literary_identity: Poet and prose writer, principally a writer of Latin-English lyric and of imaginary dialogue; one of the great English prose stylists, and a Jacobean-reviving romantic classicist rather than a participant in the Lake or Cockney schools.
biography: Landor was born in 1775 at Ipswich into a prosperous Warwickshire family, the eldest son of a doctor and a mother who died while he was young. He was sent to Rugby and then to University College, Oxford, where he was rusticated for firing a gun in his rooms and for the quarrels that followed, and where he wrote the verse that became Gebir. His marriage in 1797 to Julia Guadagni, daughter of a Florentine nobleman, brought wealth and a long domestic estrangement which ended in separation in Italy in 1819 and in the loss of access to his children, a wound he never stopped writing about. He lived chiefly in Italy, at Como, Bagni di Lucca, and above all at Bath and then at the Villa Fiesole and in Florence, with a long residence at Bath in the 1830s. In 1836 he quarrelled with his friend and patron Robert Forster, whose family he had attacked, and the resulting scandal and the loss of a share of his income shadowed his last decades. He published steadily but poorly from the 1820s, with Imaginary Conversations in 1824, Pericles and Aspasia in 1836, and the last volumes of verse in the 1860s, and he died at Florence in 1864, aged eighty-nine, leaving a large posthumous prose and verse collection.
literary_profile: His canon is small for its length of years and almost wholly made up of short or modular forms: the Spenserian romance of Gebir, the anonymous epic of The Battle of Hastings, the compact elegies, and above all the prose conversations, which he kept revising and regrouping for half a century. He wrote in a double register, English and Latin, and thought of style as the chief moral possession of a writer. His reputation rests less on any single large work than on the intensity and compression of the whole manner, and on a handful of short poems which stand outside the main currents of romanticism.
stylistic_characteristics: Austere, epigrammatic, and archaising: periods of balanced subordination, monosyllabic emphasis at the close of a passage, and a habitual refusal of transition and explanation. His dialogue dispenses with stage direction and narration, letting character appear wholly through speech, and his lyric reduces diction to the barest nouns and verbs. He is capable of extreme tenderness in the shortest space and of sustained invective in the same syntax.
intellectual_concerns: Liberty of private judgement against priest, king, and party; the claims of the affections against the family and the law; style as an ethical achievement; the study of Greek, Latin, and Italian literature as a living constitution; the moral history of tyranny and exile, and the dignity of the cultivated individual in a degraded public life.
historical_significance: He stands outside the metropolitan schools of romanticism and supplies its classical and archaising counter-tradition, handing on to later writers the imaginary conversation as a form of criticism and the short elegy as a model of condensation; his life and quarrels also document the economics and the family politics of the professional man of letters in the nineteenth century.
major_influences: the Greek lyricists and the Anacreontea
Johnson and the Augustan moralist tradition
his own reading in the Bodleian and in the Italian libraries
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of the poems of the 1790s, including the elegies addressed to Rose Aylmer, rests on manuscript evidence and on later recollection rather than on a settled chronology, and the first printing of several short pieces is imperfectly recorded.

alternative_names: Peter Porcupine (as used in his American writing)
literary_identity: Journalist, polemicist, farmer, and political historian; the greatest writer of English plebeian radical prose, and the founder of the weekly political journal as an instrument of class argument.
biography: Cobbett was born in 1763 at Goodwood near Chichester, the son of a farm bailiff, and grew up with field work, book learning, and the grammar schools within reach but not taken. He ran to sea at nineteen, married an Irish servant girl, Anne Reid, in 1791, and after a period as a clerk and a soldier, set himself up as a writer. He went to America in 1792, made his name in Philadelphia as Peter Porcupine, editor of a fiercely loyalist newspaper and of a series of pamphlets, and returned to England in 1800 disillusioned with the republic. In 1802 he founded the Political Register, which he edited almost without interruption until 1835. His imprisonment in 1810 for an attack on flogging earned him a popular martyrdom, and from the end of the war he turned his agrarianism into a systematic attack on paper credit, the funds, the taxes, and the corn laws. He fought the six Acts, defended the reformers, was repeatedly prosecuted, and in 1832 was elected to parliament for Oldham, where he spoke briefly against poor-law policy before his death at Kensington in 1835.
literary_profile: His work is at once journalistic, agricultural, historical, and autobiographical, and it was written overwhelmingly for a weekly serial audience of mechanics, small traders, and farm labourers. The Rural Rides, the currency letters, the grammar, and the polemic against the Protestant Reformation share one method: concrete observation, a documented grievance, and an appeal to the reader's own experience against 'the system'. He also wrote extensively on husbandry, on timber and planting, on style, and on education, and he was a serious editor of documents.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, Anglo-Saxon, rhythmic, and spoken: short words, direct address, repetition, and an idiom built from the workshop and the field. His prose carries invective and endearment in the same sentence, uses figures drawn from farming and from money, and treats the familiar noun as an argument in itself. He is the great English example of writing that refuses gentility without becoming colloquially vague.
intellectual_concerns: The political economy of paper money, taxation, and the national debt; the property confiscations of the Reformation as the origin of modern pauperism; the dignity and the wages of agricultural and artisanal labour; representation and corruption; the education of the labouring child in the standard language; and the defence of the small producer against both aristocracy and manufactured capital.
historical_significance: He created the popular weekly journal in England, shaped the language in which reform was argued before and after 1832, and made the condition of the labouring poor a subject of literary as well as political analysis; the documentary force of his prose is one of the two or three foundations of the social history of the romantic period.
major_influences: The eighteenth-century periodical essay and Swift
Arthur Young's farming surveys and the agricultural writers
Adam Smith and the political economists read against the grain
English Bible and Book of Common Prayer cadence
the old English chroniclers and the state-trial reporters
Franklin and the American pamphlet tradition
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his childhood schooling and of the farm where he was born are variously reported, and the extent to which the Parliamentary History and other compilations was composed by others working for him was disputed in his lifetime and remains so.
